title: Performance and Cost Optimization at Scale
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Performance and Cost Optimization at Scale ##### 40 minutes, 3 seconds, and the same data A contact-sync job took 40 minutes nightly and was creeping toward the maintenance window. The team's first instinct was a bigger server. Profiling told a different story. The job fetched 5,000 contacts, then for each one made a separate API call to fetch its company, then wrote each contact to the database individually. That is 5,000 sequential HTTP round trips at ~180 ms each (15 minutes of pure waiting), 5,000 individual `INSERT` statements, and — the detail that mattered most — 4,900 of those company lookups requested one of only **60 distinct companies**. The fix required no new hardware: batch the company lookups with a bulk endpoint, cache them by ID, run the remaining fetches with bounded concurrency, and use a single multi-row upsert. Runtime went from 40 minutes to 3 seconds. Optimization is not intuition. **Measure, find the actual bottleneck, fix that one thing, measure again.** ##### Profiling: finding the real bottleneck Four bottleneck classes cover almost all automation work. **N+1 queries and calls.** One query returns N records; then N more calls fetch each record's related data. The signature is a loop containing a network call. This is the single most common performance bug in integration code. **Sequential I/O.** Independent operations executed one at a time. If each takes 200 ms and you have 500, that is 100 seconds of mostly idle waiting. **Prompt bloat.** In AI workflows, oversized prompts dominate both latency and cost, because input tokens usually outnumber output tokens by a wide margin. **Database inefficiency.** Missing indexes, unbatched writes, and per-row round trips. Measure rather than guess: ```python import cProfile, pstats, time, contextlib @contextlib.contextmanager def timed(label: str): start = time.perf_counter() yield log.info("timing", stage=label, seconds=round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3)) # Coarse timing first — find WHICH stage is slow with timed("fetch_contacts"): contacts = fetch_contacts() with timed("enrich_companies"): enriched = enrich(contacts) with timed("write_db"): write(enriched) # Then profile the slow stage specifically profiler = cProfile.Profile() profiler.enable() enrich(contacts[:100]) profiler.disable() pstats.Stats(profiler).sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(15) ``` For distributed pipelines, OpenTelemetry traces give you the same information across services — one flame graph showing exactly which hop consumed the time. ##### Batching and bulk endpoints The highest-return fix, almost always. ```python # BEFORE: N+1 — 5,000 sequential calls, ~15 minutes for contact in contacts: company = api.get_company(contact["company_id"]) # one round trip each contact["company_name"] = company["name"] # AFTER: deduplicate, then one bulk call per 100 — ~2 seconds unique_ids = list({c["company_id"] for c in contacts if c.get("company_id")}) companies: dict[str, dict] = {} for i in range(0, len(unique_ids), 100): batch = unique_ids[i:i + 100] companies.update({c["id"]: c for c in api.get_companies_bulk(batch)}) for contact in contacts: contact["company_name"] = companies.get(contact["company_id"], {}).get("name") ``` Two wins compound here: **deduplication** (60 lookups instead of 5,000) and **batching** (one request per 100 instead of one per item). Always check whether an API offers a bulk or `ids=` endpoint before writing a loop. The same applies to database writes: ```python # BEFORE: 5,000 round trips for c in contacts: cur.execute("INSERT INTO contacts (id, email, name) VALUES (%s,%s,%s) " "ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET email=EXCLUDED.email", (c["id"], c["email"], c["name"])) # AFTER: one statement per 1,000 rows from psycopg.extras import execute_values execute_values(cur, """INSERT INTO contacts (id, email, name) VALUES %s ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email, name = EXCLUDED.name""", [(c["id"], c["email"], c["name"]) for c in contacts], page_size=1000) ``` ##### Parallelization with bounded concurrency When no bulk endpoint exists, run calls concurrently — but **bounded**, or you will exhaust sockets and trip rate limits. ```python import asyncio, httpx async def fetch_all(ids: list[str], concurrency: int = 20) -> list[dict]: limits = httpx.Limits(max_connections=concurrency, max_keepalive_connections=concurrency) sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency) async with httpx.AsyncClient(limits=limits, timeout=10) as client: async def one(item_id: str) -> dict | None: async with sem: # the bound try: r = await client.get(f"{BASE}/items/{item_id}") r.raise_for_status() return r.json() except httpx.HTTPError as exc: log.warning("fetch_failed", id=item_id, error=str(exc)) return None results = await asyncio.gather(*(one(i) for i in ids)) return [r for r in results if r is not None] ``` Tune concurrency against the **provider's rate limit**, not your machine's capacity. If the API allows 600 requests/minute, that is 10/second — running 50 concurrent requests just means you collect 429s faster. Compute the ceiling: `concurrency ≈ rate_limit_per_second × average_latency_seconds`. For CPU-bound work (parsing, image processing), asyncio does not help — use `ProcessPoolExecutor` or push the work to more workers. ##### Caching and connection pooling **Caching** turns repeated work into a lookup. Match the layer to the volatility: | Layer | Use for | TTL | |---|---|---| | In-process (`lru_cache`) | Reference data within one run | Process lifetime | | Redis | Cross-process, cross-run lookups | Minutes to hours | | HTTP conditional (`ETag`) | Large payloads that rarely change | Server-controlled | | Materialized view | Expensive aggregate queries | Refresh schedule | **Connection pooling** is frequently overlooked and costs real milliseconds. Establishing a TCP connection plus TLS handshake takes 50–200 ms; a pooled connection reuses it. Use one `httpx.Client` or `requests.Session` for the life of the process, not one per call — that change alone often halves the time of a chatty integration. Same for the database: a pool sized to your worker concurrency, not a new connection per query. ##### Database performance at volume The three levers, in order of impact: **Indexes on filter, join and sort columns.** Verify with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and look for `Seq Scan` on large tables. Partial indexes shine on queue tables where only a small subset is ever queried. **Bulk operations** — `execute_values`, or `COPY` for very large loads, which is dramatically faster than any `INSERT` form. **Query shape.** Avoid `SELECT *` in hot paths (it prevents index-only scans), push filtering into SQL rather than Python, and use `LIMIT` with keyset pagination rather than deep `OFFSET`. ##### Load testing with k6 Optimizing without load testing means guessing at your ceiling. ```javascript // loadtest.js import http from 'k6/http'; import { check, sleep } from 'k6'; import { Trend, Rate } from 'k6/metrics'; const processingTime = new Trend('processing_time'); const errorRate = new Rate('errors'); export const options = { stages: [ { duration: '1m', target: 20 }, // ramp up { duration: '3m', target: 20 }, // steady state — read metrics HERE { duration: '1m', target: 100 }, // spike: find the breaking point { duration: '2m', target: 100 }, { duration: '1m', target: 0 }, // ramp down ], thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(95)<1000', 'p(99)<3000'], errors: ['rate<0.01'], }, }; export default function () { const payload = JSON.stringify({ event_id: `evt_${__VU}_${__ITER}`, // unique per request type: 'order.paid', data: { order_id: `ORD-${__VU}-${__ITER}`, amount_total: 499800 }, }); const res = http.post(`${__ENV.TARGET}/webhooks/orders`, payload, { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'X-Signature': __ENV.SIG }, }); check(res, { 'accepted': (r) => r.status === 202, 'fast ack': (r) => r.timings.duration < 200, }) || errorRate.add(1); processingTime.add(res.timings.duration); sleep(0.5); } ``` Run it, watch your Grafana dashboard simultaneously, and identify what saturates first — CPU, database connections, queue depth, or an external rate limit. **The bottleneck is almost never where you assumed.** Locust is the Python-native alternative if you prefer writing scenarios in Python. ##### Platform economics The cost model differs fundamentally by platform, and modelling it is a core intermediate skill. ```text WORKFLOW: order processing, 9 billable steps, 10,000 runs/month ZAPIER (per task ≈ per action step) 10,000 × 9 = 90,000 tasks Requires a high tier; roughly $289–599/mo depending on plan → ≈ ₹24,000–50,000/month MAKE.COM (per operation = module × bundle) 10,000 × 9 = 90,000 operations (plus bundle multiplication if iterating) Mid tier ≈ $34–99/mo → ≈ ₹2,800–8,200/month SELF-HOSTED n8n (per execution is free; you pay for infrastructure) 10,000 executions — node count irrelevant VPS (4 vCPU/8 GB) ≈ ₹2,000/mo Managed Postgres ≈ ₹1,200/mo Backups + monitoring ≈ ₹500/mo Engineering time: ~2 h/month × ₹1,500 = ₹3,000 → ≈ ₹6,700/month all-in n8n CLOUD (per execution) 10,000 executions ≈ $50–120/mo → ₹4,200–10,000/month ``` Three lessons from the arithmetic. **Step count drives Zapier and Make costs but not n8n's**, so long workflows change the ranking. **Self-hosting is not free** — include engineering time, or the comparison is dishonest. And **the crossover moves with volume**: at 500 runs/month Zapier is cheapest in total cost of ownership because the operational overhead dominates; at 50,000 it is not close. Always model with **your actual step count and volume**, add 30% headroom for retries and growth, and re-check annually. ##### Concurrency and rate-limit tuning The final tuning loop, and the parameters interact: - **Worker concurrency** — raise until the database, the external API, or CPU saturates. For I/O-bound work, 10–20 per worker; for CPU-bound, match core count. - **Database pool size** — `workers × pool_size` must stay under Postgres `max_connections`. Use PgBouncer when that becomes binding. - **External rate limits** — throttle proactively below the ceiling rather than colliding with it. - **Batch size** — larger batches amortize overhead but increase memory, retry cost and timeout risk. 100–1,000 is usually the sweet spot. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Load test with k6] --> B[Read dashboard:
what saturates first?] B --> C{Bottleneck} C -->|N+1 calls| D[Deduplicate + bulk endpoint] C -->|sequential I/O| E[Bounded concurrency] C -->|per-row DB writes| F[execute_values / COPY] C -->|slow queries| G[Index + EXPLAIN ANALYZE] C -->|repeated lookups| H[Cache + connection pooling] C -->|LLM cost/latency| I[Trim prompt, smaller model, cache] D & E & F & G & H & I --> J[Re-measure] J --> K{Target met?} K -->|no| A K -->|yes| L[Model cost per 10k runs
across platforms] ``` ##### Common pitfalls - **Optimizing without profiling** — fixing the wrong thing. - **Network calls inside loops** — the N+1 signature. - **Unbounded parallelism**, causing 429s and socket exhaustion. - **A new HTTP client or DB connection per call.** - **Micro-optimizing Python** when 95% of the time is network wait. - **Batch sizes so large** that one failure retries thousands of records. - **Caching without a TTL or invalidation strategy**, serving stale data. - **Load testing only the happy path**, missing behaviour under partial failure. - **Comparing platform costs on price alone**, ignoring engineering time. - **Tuning concurrency to your machine** rather than the provider's rate limit. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **load-test a workflow with k6**, find the bottleneck, **batch and parallelize** it, then **model cost per 10,000 runs across Zapier, Make and self-hosted n8n** and recommend the cheapest. Record before/after numbers for throughput, p95 latency and resource usage — the measurement is the deliverable, not the optimization. The mini project focuses the engineering half: load test, identify the bottleneck, apply batching plus bounded parallelization, and **measure the throughput and latency improvement**. Change one thing at a time and re-measure, so you can attribute the gain. "Batching the company lookups took us from 40 minutes to 4; adding concurrency took 4 minutes to 3 seconds" is a far more useful result than a single combined number. For the assignment, **model the cost per 10,000 runs on all three platforms for one real workflow** and recommend the cheapest. Include engineering time for the self-hosted option and state your assumptions explicitly — step count, retry rate, growth headroom. Then note where the recommendation would flip: at what volume does the ranking change? That sensitivity analysis is what makes it an engineering recommendation rather than a price quote. ##### Key takeaways - Profile before optimizing — the bottleneck is usually N+1 calls, sequential I/O, per-row database writes, or prompt bloat, not raw compute. - Deduplicate and batch first; it routinely delivers order-of-magnitude wins with no infrastructure change. - Parallelize with a bound derived from the provider's rate limit, and reuse pooled HTTP and database connections rather than creating them per call. - Load test with k6 while watching your metrics dashboard, and find what saturates first rather than assuming. - Model platform cost with your real step count and volume, include engineering time for self-hosting, and identify the volume at which the cheapest option changes.
